Medicine-01.question: ১) Cause of Right iliac fossa mass is?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is caecal carcinoma. A mass in the right iliac fossa is classically associated with a caecal tumour because the caecum is located in the right iliac fossa.

Common causes of right iliac fossa (RIF) mass:

  • Caecal carcinoma ✓

  • Appendicular mass

  • Crohn’s disease mass

  • Ileocaecal tuberculosis

  • Psoas abscess

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sigmoid colon cancer → Usually presents with a left iliac fossa mass.

  • Constipation → May cause fecal loading but not a typical RIF mass.

  • Diverticular mass → Usually affects sigmoid colon and causes left-sided mass.

High-yield surgery recall:

RIF mass → Caecal carcinoma / Appendicular mass / Crohn’s / Ileocaecal TB
LIF mass → Sigmoid colon pathology

Exam pearl:
Caecal carcinoma is the classic colonic tumour presenting as a right iliac fossa mass.

Medicine-01.question: ২) Which enzyme is responsible for hydrolytic type of pancreatic secration?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is acetylcholine. Hydrolytic enzyme secretion from pancreatic acinar cells is mainly stimulated by acetylcholine (ACh) via vagal stimulation.

Key points:

  • Pancreatic acinar cells → Enzymes (hydrolytic secretion)

    • Stimulated by:

      • Acetylcholine (major)

      • CCK

  • Pancreatic duct cells → Bicarbonate secretion

    • Stimulated by:

      • Secretin

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CCK → Stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction, but ACh is the classic neural stimulant.

  • Secretin → Stimulates bicarbonate-rich pancreatic secretion.

  • VIP → Causes intestinal water/electrolyte secretion and relaxation of smooth muscle.

High-yield GI recall:

Acinar cells → Enzymes → ACh + CCK
Duct cells → HCO₃⁻ → Secretin

Exam pearl:
Hydrolytic pancreatic enzyme secretion = Acetylcholine (vagal stimulation).

Medicine-01.question: ৩) Which hormone is secreted from Throughout GIT?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is somatostatin. Somatostatin is secreted by D cells located throughout the gastrointestinal tract (especially stomach, intestine) and pancreas.

Key points:

  • Somatostatin (D cells):

    • Present throughout GIT

    • Inhibits:

      • Gastrin secretion

      • Insulin secretion

      • Pancreatic and intestinal secretion

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gastrin → Secreted mainly from G cells of gastric antrum.

  • Cholecystokinin (CCK) → Secreted from I cells of duodenum and jejunum.

  • Secretin → Secreted from S cells of duodenum.

High-yield GI hormone recall:

Hormone Source
Gastrin G cells (gastric antrum)
Somatostatin D cells throughout GIT
CCK I cells (duodenum/jejunum)
Secretin S cells (duodenum)

Exam pearl:
Hormone distributed throughout GIT = Somatostatin.

Medicine-01.question: ৪) Which of the following isn’t a Alarm features in dyspepsia?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is hematuria. Hematuria is not an alarm feature of dyspepsia; it suggests a urinary tract pathology rather than upper gastrointestinal disease.

Alarm features in dyspepsia include:

  • Unintentional weight loss ✓

  • Anaemia ✓

  • Persistent vomiting ✓

  • Progressive dysphagia

  • Gastrointestinal bleeding (haematemesis/melaena)

  • Family history of upper GI cancer

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Weight loss → Alarm feature.

  • Anaemia → Alarm feature suggesting possible GI bleeding or malignancy.

  • Vomiting → Alarm feature, especially persistent vomiting.

High-yield GI recall:

Dyspepsia alarm features → Weight loss + Anaemia + Vomiting + Dysphagia + GI bleeding

Exam pearl:
Hematuria is not an alarm feature of dyspepsia.

Medicine-01.question: ৫) Which of the following is the most common GIT emergency?
Medicine-01.option4: Subacute or chronic lower gastrointestinal bleeding
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (UGIH). Acute upper GI bleeding is the most common gastrointestinal emergency encountered in clinical practice.

Common causes:

  • Peptic ulcer disease (most common)

  • Oesophageal varices

  • Gastritis/duodenitis

  • Mallory–Weiss tear

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Severe acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding → Less common than upper GI bleeding.

  • Chronic occult gastrointestinal bleeding → Usually presents with iron deficiency anaemia, not as an emergency.

  • Subacute or chronic lower gastrointestinal bleeding → Not considered a common GI emergency.

High-yield GI recall:

Most common GI emergency → Acute upper GI haemorrhage
Most common cause of upper GI bleeding → Peptic ulcer disease

Exam pearl:
Acute upper GI haemorrhage is the commonest GIT emergency.

Medicine-01.question: ৬) Elevated blood urea with normal creatinine concentration implies
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is severe bleeding. An elevated blood urea with a normal creatinine level suggests increased urea production, classically seen in upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Mechanism:

  • Blood proteins are digested in the intestine → increased amino acid absorption → increased hepatic urea production → raised blood urea

  • Renal function remains normal → normal creatinine

The other options are incorrect because:

  • AKI → Usually causes elevation of both urea and creatinine.

  • Impaired liver function → Decreases urea synthesis, causing low urea.

  • Ca stomach → May cause bleeding but is not the typical explanation for isolated raised urea.

High-yield GI recall:

High urea + normal creatinine → Upper GI bleeding
High urea + high creatinine → Renal impairment

Exam pearl:
Raised urea disproportionate to creatinine is a clue to upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

Medicine-01.question: ৭) Which one of the following is the most common cause of Upper GIT bleeding?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is peptic ulcer disease. Peptic ulcer is the most common cause of upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding.

Common causes of upper GIT bleeding:

  1. Peptic ulcer disease ✓ (most common)

  2. Oesophageal/gastric varices

  3. Gastritis and gastric erosions

  4. Mallory–Weiss tear

  5. Oesophagitis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Varices → Important cause, especially in portal hypertension, but less common than peptic ulcers.

  • Esophagitis → Can cause bleeding but is less frequent.

  • Gastric erosions → Cause acute bleeding but less common than peptic ulcer.

High-yield GI recall:

Most common cause of upper GI bleeding = Peptic ulcer disease
Massive upper GI bleed in cirrhosis = Varices

Exam pearl:
Peptic ulcer disease is the leading cause of upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage.

Medicine-01.question: ৮) Which one of the following is the most common cause of Chronic or relapsing diarrhea?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). IBS is the most common cause of chronic or relapsing diarrhoea, especially when there is no evidence of organic bowel disease.

Key points:

  • IBS (diarrhoea-predominant type, IBS-D):

    • Chronic/recurrent diarrhoea

    • Abdominal pain related to defecation

    • Altered bowel habit

    • No structural abnormality

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IBD (Crohn’s disease/Ulcerative colitis) → Causes chronic diarrhoea but is less common than IBS.

  • Giardiasis → Causes persistent diarrhoea, especially with contaminated water exposure, but is not the most common overall.

  • Ca rectum → May cause altered bowel habit but is not a common cause of chronic relapsing diarrhoea.

High-yield GI recall:

Most common cause of chronic relapsing diarrhoea → IBS
Inflammatory diarrhoea with blood → IBD
Persistent watery diarrhoea after travel → Giardia

Exam pearl:
IBS is the commonest cause of recurrent/chronic diarrhoeal symptoms in the community.

Medicine-01.question: ৯) Diarrhoea and weight loss in patients with a normal diet are likely to be caused by which of the following condition?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is malabsorption. Chronic diarrhoea with weight loss despite a normal diet suggests failure of absorption of nutrients from the small intestine.

Features of malabsorption syndrome:

  • Chronic diarrhoea

  • Weight loss

  • Steatorrhoea (fatty stool)

  • Nutritional deficiencies

  • Anaemia (e.g., iron, B12 deficiency)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IBS → Causes chronic diarrhoea but typically does not cause weight loss or nutritional deficiency.

  • Small bowel → Incomplete option; small bowel diseases may cause malabsorption, but the condition itself is the answer.

  • Large bowel malignancy → May cause altered bowel habit and weight loss, but not the classic combination with normal diet.

High-yield GI recall:

Diarrhoea + weight loss + normal food intake → Malabsorption
Diarrhoea without weight loss → IBS more likely

Exam pearl:
Weight loss in chronic diarrhoea suggests organic disease, especially malabsorption.

Medicine-01.question: ১০) All of the following GIT disease Causes weight loss except..
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is IBS (Irritable bowel syndrome). IBS typically does not cause weight loss because it is a functional gastrointestinal disorder without malabsorption or inflammation.

The other options can cause weight loss:

  • Dysphagia ✓ → Reduced food intake leading to weight loss.

  • Malabsorption ✓ → Nutrient loss and poor absorption cause weight loss.

  • IBD (Crohn’s disease/Ulcerative colitis) ✓ → Chronic inflammation, reduced intake, and malabsorption can cause weight loss.

  • IBS ✗ → Usually no weight loss; weight loss is an alarm feature suggesting another diagnosis.

High-yield GI recall:

IBS → No weight loss
Weight loss + diarrhoea → Think organic disease (IBD, malignancy, malabsorption)

Exam pearl:
Weight loss is an alarm feature that argues against IBS.

Medicine-01.question: ১১) Chronic gastric ulcers caused by H.pylori are mostly situated in which of the following area?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is lesser curve. Chronic gastric ulcers associated with H. pylori infection are most commonly located along the lesser curvature of the stomach, near the incisura angularis.

Key points:

  • Chronic gastric ulcer (H. pylori related):

    • Common site → Lesser curvature

    • Particularly near the incisura angularis

    • Associated with antral gastritis and increased acid exposure

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fundus → Rare site for gastric ulcer.

  • Greater curve → Less common; ulcers here may raise suspicion for malignancy.

  • Body → Can be affected but less typical than lesser curvature.

High-yield GI recall:

Gastric ulcer → Lesser curvature (incisura angularis)
Duodenal ulcer → First part of duodenum (anterior wall)

Exam pearl:
H. pylori chronic gastric ulcer classically occurs on the lesser curvature.

Medicine-01.question: ১২) A middle aged female comes to you with persistent daily vomiting, what will be the cause?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is gastric outlet obstruction. Persistent daily vomiting is a classic feature of gastric outlet obstruction due to impaired emptying of gastric contents.

Common causes:

  • Peptic ulcer disease causing pyloric/duodenal scarring (common benign cause)

  • Gastric carcinoma

  • Pancreatic malignancy

Clinical features:

  • Persistent non-bilious vomiting

  • Early satiety

  • Abdominal distension

  • Weight loss

  • Succussion splash

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Peptic ulcer disease → May cause nausea and vomiting, but persistent daily vomiting suggests obstruction or complicated disease.

  • Non-ulcer dyspepsia → Causes upper abdominal discomfort, bloating, early satiety; persistent vomiting is an alarm feature.

  • Gastric erosion → Usually causes pain or bleeding, not chronic vomiting.

High-yield GI recall:

Persistent vomiting + weight loss → Gastric outlet obstruction
Dyspepsia + alarm feature (vomiting) → Endoscopy required

Exam pearl:
Daily persistent vomiting in a middle-aged patient suggests gastric outlet obstruction until proven otherwise.

Medicine-01.question: ১৩) Which of the following is the Preferred investigation for peptic ulcer disease?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (OGD). Upper GI endoscopy is the preferred investigation for peptic ulcer disease because it directly visualizes the ulcer, allows biopsy, and helps exclude malignancy.

Key advantages:

  • Direct visualization of gastric and duodenal mucosa

  • Biopsy of gastric ulcers to rule out cancer

  • Can perform H. pylori testing (e.g., rapid urease test from biopsy)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rapid urease test → Detects H. pylori from endoscopic biopsy; not the primary investigation for diagnosing an ulcer.

  • Urea breath test → Non-invasive test for H. pylori infection, useful for confirmation of eradication.

  • Culture → Rarely used; mainly for antibiotic sensitivity studies.

High-yield GI recall:

Peptic ulcer disease → Upper GI endoscopy (OGD) is the investigation of choice
H. pylori detection → Urea breath test / Rapid urease test

Exam pearl:
Endoscopy is preferred in PUD because it detects ulcer + allows biopsy.

Medicine-01.question: ১৪) Which of the following condition isn’t associated with H.pylori infection?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is GERD. H. pylori infection is not considered a cause of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. In fact, eradication of H. pylori may slightly increase the risk of GERD symptoms in some patients.

Conditions associated with H. pylori infection:

  • Peptic ulcer disease ✓

  • Gastric carcinoma ✓

  • Chronic gastritis / Pangastritis ✓

  • Gastric MALT lymphoma ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Peptic ulcer disease → Strong association with H. pylori.

  • Gastric carcinoma → H. pylori is a major risk factor (WHO class I carcinogen).

  • Pangastritis → H. pylori can cause chronic active gastritis involving the entire stomach.

High-yield GI recall:

H. pylori → Peptic ulcer + Gastritis + Gastric cancer + MALT lymphoma
Not associated → GERD

Exam pearl:
H. pylori is linked to gastric pathology, not reflux disease.

Medicine-01.question: ১৫) Which of the following condition is indicated for emergency surgery in peptic ulcer disease?
Medicine-01.option2: Persistent ulceration despite adequate medical therapy
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is haemorrhage. Severe uncontrolled bleeding from a peptic ulcer is an indication for emergency surgery if endoscopic and medical measures fail.

Emergency indications for surgery in peptic ulcer disease:

  • Massive or uncontrolled haemorrhage ✓

  • Perforation with peritonitis ✓

  • Gastric outlet obstruction (usually elective surgery)

  • Refractory or recurrent ulcers (usually elective)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gastric outflow obstruction → Usually requires elective surgical management after initial correction of fluid/electrolyte imbalance.

  • Persistent ulceration despite adequate medical therapy → Indication for elective surgery, not emergency.

  • Recurrent ulcer following gastric surgery → Usually managed electively.

High-yield GI recall:

Emergency surgery in PUD → Bleeding + Perforation
Elective surgery → Obstruction + Refractory/recurrent ulcer

Exam pearl:
Uncontrolled haemorrhage is the classic emergency surgical indication in peptic ulcer disease.

Medicine-01.question: ১৬) Drugs used in rescue therapy for H. pylori eraditacion excludes?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Clarithromycin. Rescue (salvage) therapy for H. pylori eradication usually avoids antibiotics previously used in first-line therapy, especially clarithromycin, due to increasing resistance.

Common rescue therapy options include:

  • Levofloxacin ✓ (levofloxacin-based triple therapy)

  • Amoxicillin ✓

  • PPI ✓

  • Bismuth-containing quadruple therapy

The other option:

  • Clarithromycin ✗ → Usually avoided in rescue therapy if prior macrolide exposure or failure of clarithromycin-based therapy because of resistance.

High-yield GI recall:

First-line H. pylori therapy → PPI + Amoxicillin + Clarithromycin (where resistance is low)
Rescue therapy → PPI + Amoxicillin + Levofloxacin / Bismuth-based regimen

Exam pearl:
Clarithromycin is generally excluded from salvage therapy after eradication failure.

Medicine-01.question: ১৭) Which type metabolic abnormality occurs in Gastric outlet obstruction as a consequence of PUD?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis. Gastric outlet obstruction causes persistent vomiting of gastric hydrochloric acid (HCl), leading to loss of hydrogen ions and chloride ions.

Mechanism:

  • Loss of H⁺ → Metabolic alkalosis

  • Loss of Cl⁻ → Hypochloraemia

  • Volume depletion → activates RAAS → increased renal bicarbonate retention

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypochloraemic metabolic acidosis → Not expected with loss of gastric acid.

  • Hyperchloraemic metabolic alkalosis → Chloride is lost, so chloride level decreases.

  • Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis → Seen in bicarbonate loss (e.g., diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis).

High-yield GI recall:

Gastric outlet obstruction → Vomiting → Loss of HCl → Hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis

Exam pearl:
Persistent vomiting causes “chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis.”

Medicine-01.question: ১৮) In a case of abdominal Tuberculosis, which area is most commonly affected?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is ileocaecal region. Abdominal tuberculosis most commonly affects the ileocaecal junction due to physiological stasis, abundant lymphoid tissue, and increased absorption time allowing bacilli to penetrate the mucosa.

Common sites of abdominal TB:

  • Ileocaecal region ✓ (most common)

  • Jejunum

  • Colon

  • Peritoneum

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Duodenum → Rarely involved due to rapid transit and protective factors.

  • Caecum → Frequently involved but the classic site is the ileocaecal region.

  • Colon → May be involved but less commonly than ileocaecal area.

High-yield GI recall:

Abdominal TB → Ileocaecal region (most common site)
Most common extra-pulmonary TB site → Lymph node

Exam pearl:
Ileocaecal junction is the favourite site of intestinal tuberculosis.

Medicine-01.question: ১৯) In a case of abdominal Tuberculosis, treatment should be continued for...
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is 6 months. Abdominal tuberculosis is treated with the standard anti-tuberculous regimen for 6 months, similar to pulmonary TB in most cases.

Treatment regimen:

  • Intensive phase (2 months):
    HRZE → Isoniazid + Rifampicin + Pyrazinamide + Ethambutol

  • Continuation phase (4 months):
    HR → Isoniazid + Rifampicin

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 4 months → Too short for standard TB treatment.

  • 8 months → Not routinely required for abdominal TB.

  • 12 months → Reserved for selected complicated cases (e.g., CNS TB, bone TB), not routine abdominal TB.

High-yield TB recall:

Abdominal TB treatment duration = 6 months
Regimen = 2HRZE + 4HR

Exam pearl:
Intestinal/abdominal tuberculosis is treated with the standard 6-month anti-TB regimen.

Medicine-01.question: ২০) Which is not a histological features of Ulcerative colitis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is numerous goblet cells. Ulcerative colitis typically shows goblet cell depletion due to chronic inflammation, not an increase in goblet cells.

Histological features of ulcerative colitis:

  • Crypt distortion ✓

  • Cryptitis ✓ (neutrophil infiltration of crypt epithelium)

  • Crypt abscesses ✓ (neutrophil accumulation within crypt lumen)

  • Goblet cell depletion ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Crypt distortion → Due to chronic mucosal inflammation and regeneration.

  • Cryptitis → Characteristic active inflammation.

  • Crypt abscesses → Typical microscopic feature of UC.

High-yield GI pathology recall:

Ulcerative colitis → Mucosal disease + crypt distortion + crypt abscess + goblet cell depletion
Crohn’s disease → Transmural inflammation + granuloma + skip lesions

Exam pearl:
Goblet cell depletion, not numerous goblet cells, is seen in ulcerative colitis.

Medicine-01.question: ২১) Which disease is greatly associated with Ulcerative colitis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC is the most important hepatobiliary disease associated with ulcerative colitis.

Key points:

  • PSC ↔ Ulcerative colitis

    • Strong association

    • Inflammation and fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts

    • Increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma

The other options are incorrect because:

  • PBC (Primary biliary cholangitis) → Associated with autoimmune diseases but not strongly linked with UC.

  • Autoimmune hepatitis → Can coexist with autoimmune disorders but not a classic UC association.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) → Autoimmune disease but not specifically associated with UC.

High-yield GI recall:

Ulcerative colitis extraintestinal association:

  • PSC (classic)

  • Arthritis

  • Uveitis

  • Erythema nodosum

  • Pyoderma gangrenosum

Exam pearl:
UC + cholestatic liver disease = Think PSC.

Medicine-01.question: ২২) In a case of Crohn's disease, which area is commonly affected?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is ileal or ileocolonic involvement. The terminal ileum, with or without colonic involvement, is the most common site affected in Crohn’s disease.

Common distribution of Crohn’s disease:

  • Ileocolonic disease → most common ✓

  • Small intestine (particularly terminal ileum)

  • Colon

  • Perianal disease (important complication)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Small intestinal → Can be affected, but isolated small bowel disease is less common than ileocolonic disease.

  • Colon → May be involved but not the most common pattern.

  • Perianal → Occurs as a complication, not the primary common site.

High-yield GI recall:

Crohn’s disease → Terminal ileum ± colon (ileocolonic)
Ulcerative colitis → Colon only (starting from rectum)

Exam pearl:
Most common site of Crohn’s disease = terminal ileum with ileocaecal involvement.

Medicine-01.question: ২৩) Which one of the following is the cardinal symptom of Ulcerative colitis?
Medicine-01.option3: rectal bleeding with passage of mucus
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is rectal bleeding with passage of mucus. The cardinal symptom of ulcerative colitis is bloody diarrhoea with mucus due to continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon and rectum.

Typical features of ulcerative colitis:

  • Bloody diarrhoea with mucus ✓

  • Increased stool frequency

  • Urgency and tenesmus

  • Lower abdominal cramps

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Abdominal pain → May occur but is not the cardinal symptom.

  • Watery diarrhoea → More typical of secretory/infectious causes; UC diarrhoea is usually bloody.

  • Vomiting → Not a typical feature of UC.

High-yield GI recall:

Ulcerative colitis → Bloody mucus diarrhoea + urgency + tenesmus
Crohn’s disease → Chronic diarrhoea + abdominal pain + weight loss

Exam pearl:
Cardinal symptom of UC = Rectal bleeding with mucus discharge.

Medicine-01.question: ২৪) Followings are the major symptoms of Crohn’s disease, excludes..
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is bloody diarrhoea. Bloody diarrhoea is more characteristic of ulcerative colitis than Crohn’s disease.

Major symptoms of Crohn’s disease:

  • Abdominal pain ✓ (common, especially right lower quadrant)

  • Watery diarrhoea ✓

  • Weight loss ✓

  • Fatigue, fever

  • Perianal disease/fistulae

The other option:

  • Bloody diarrhoea ✗ → Can occur in Crohn’s colitis, but is classically associated with ulcerative colitis.

High-yield GI recall:

Crohn’s disease → Abdominal pain + watery diarrhoea + weight loss
Ulcerative colitis → Bloody diarrhoea with mucus + urgency

Exam pearl:
Bloody diarrhoea = Think UC first; watery diarrhoea = Think Crohn’s.

Medicine-01.question: ২৫) Which of the following feature is reralted to the activity of inflammatory bowel disease?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is conjunctivitis. Ocular manifestations such as conjunctivitis/episcleritis are extraintestinal features that often correlate with the activity of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

IBD extraintestinal manifestations:

  • Related to intestinal disease activity:

    • Conjunctivitis ✓

    • Episcleritis

    • Peripheral arthritis

  • Usually independent of disease activity:

    • Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)

    • Ankylosing spondylitis

    • Uveitis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Autoimmune hepatitis → Not a typical IBD activity-related manifestation.

  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis → Strongly associated with UC but usually does not parallel bowel activity.

  • Gallstones → Associated especially with Crohn’s disease due to ileal involvement, but not related to IBD activity.

High-yield GI recall:

IBD activity-related → Conjunctivitis, episcleritis, peripheral arthritis
IBD activity-independent → PSC, uveitis, ankylosing spondylitis

Exam pearl:
Conjunctivitis is an extraintestinal manifestation that reflects IBD activity.

Medicine-01.question: ২৬) Which of the followings isn’t a feature of IBS?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is structural abnormality. Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder without any structural abnormality on investigation.

Features of IBS:

  • Recurrent abdominal pain ✓

  • Altered bowel habit / abnormal defecation ✓

  • Symptoms worsened by stress ✓

  • Normal structural examination ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Recurrent abdominal pain → Core feature of IBS (Rome IV criteria).

  • Abnormal defecation → Common feature due to altered bowel habits.

  • Worsening of symptoms by stress → Common trigger in IBS.

High-yield GI recall:

IBS = Functional disorder → No structural abnormality
IBD = Inflammatory disease → Structural mucosal changes

Exam pearl:
Presence of structural abnormality suggests organic disease, not IBS.

Medicine-01.question: ২৭) Which of the followings is the best treatment option after diagnosis of IBS?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is reassurance. IBS is a functional gastrointestinal disorder, and after confirming the diagnosis, reassurance, education, and lifestyle modification are the cornerstone of management.

Management of IBS:

  • Reassurance and explanation of the benign nature of the disease ✓

  • Dietary modification (e.g., low FODMAP diet in selected patients)

  • Stress management

  • Symptom-directed therapy if needed

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 5-ASA → Used mainly for inflammatory bowel disease (especially ulcerative colitis), not IBS.

  • Amitriptyline → May be used as a second-line option in IBS with significant pain or diarrhoea, but not the best initial treatment.

  • Loperamide → May help diarrhoea-predominant IBS but only treats a symptom.

High-yield GI recall:

IBS first-line treatment → Reassurance + lifestyle/diet modification
IBD → Anti-inflammatory therapy (e.g., 5-ASA, steroids, biologics)

Exam pearl:
The most important initial treatment after IBS diagnosis is reassurance.

Medicine-01.question: ২৮) Which one isn’t correct regarding Glasgow criteria for prognosis of acute pancratitis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) > 600 U/L. In the Glasgow (Imrie) criteria for acute pancreatitis prognosis, the LDH threshold is >600 IU/L, not >600 U/L as a separate criterion; however, this option is considered incorrect due to unit mismatch in standard criteria.

Glasgow criteria (PANCREAS) for severe acute pancreatitis:

  • P → PaO₂ < 8 kPa (60 mmHg) ✓

  • A → Age >55 years (not >50) ✓

  • N → Neutrophilia

  • C → Calcium <2 mmol/L

  • R → Renal impairment (urea >16 mmol/L)

  • E → Enzymes (LDH >600 IU/L, AST >200 IU/L)

  • A → Albumin <32 g/L

  • S → Sugar (glucose >10 mmol/L)

Important correction:

  • Age >50 years is not the classic Glasgow criterion; the accepted cut-off is age >55 years.

Therefore, among the given options, the best answer is:

✅ ক) Age > 50 years

High-yield recall:
Glasgow criteria: Age >55, PO₂ <60 mmHg, Glucose >10 mmol/L, LDH >600 IU/L.

Medicine-01.question: ২৯) Which one of the following is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is gallstones. Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis worldwide.

Mechanism:

  • Gallstone passes through the common bile duct

  • Causes obstruction at the ampulla of Vater

  • Leads to pancreatic duct obstruction and activation of pancreatic enzymes → pancreatitis

Common causes of acute pancreatitis:

  1. Gallstones ✓ (most common)

  2. Alcohol

  3. Hypertriglyceridaemia

  4. Drugs

  5. Post-ERCP

  6. Idiopathic causes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Alcohol → One of the most common causes, especially in Western countries, but generally second to gallstones.

  • Idiopathic causes → Diagnosis made when no cause is identified; not the most common.

  • Post-ERCP → Important iatrogenic cause but relatively uncommon.

High-yield GI recall:

Acute pancreatitis → Gallstones + Alcohol (top two causes)
Worldwide most common cause = Gallstones

Exam pearl:
Gallstones are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis.

Medicine-01.question: ৩০) Which one is the confirmatory investigation of acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is serum lipase. A raised serum lipase level is the preferred confirmatory biochemical test for acute pancreatitis because it is more specific and remains elevated longer than amylase.

Diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis (need 2 of 3):

  1. Typical abdominal pain ✓

  2. Serum lipase (or amylase) >3 times upper limit of normal ✓

  3. Imaging evidence of pancreatitis ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. amylase → Can diagnose pancreatitis but is less specific and returns to normal earlier.

  • USG → Useful mainly to identify gallstones and biliary cause, not the confirmatory test.

  • MRCP → Used for biliary/pancreatic duct evaluation, not routine diagnosis.

High-yield GI recall:

Best confirmatory test for acute pancreatitis = Serum lipase
Amylase = less specific
USG = find gallstones

Exam pearl:
Serum lipase is the preferred biochemical marker for acute pancreatitis.

Medicine-01.question: ৩১) Which one is the gold standard investigation for pancreatic function assesment?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is secretin stimulation test. The secretin stimulation test is considered the gold standard for assessing exocrine pancreatic function.

Mechanism:

  • Secretin stimulates pancreatic duct cells to release bicarbonate-rich fluid.

  • The collected duodenal fluid is analysed for bicarbonate concentration.

  • It assesses pancreatic exocrine reserve, especially in chronic pancreatitis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pancreolauryl test → Non-invasive indirect test of pancreatic exocrine function, less commonly used.

  • Faecal pancreatic elastase → Commonly used non-invasive screening test for pancreatic insufficiency, but not the gold standard.

  • MRCP → Imaging test for pancreatic duct anatomy, not functional assessment.

High-yield GI recall:

Gold standard for pancreatic exocrine function → Secretin stimulation test
Common non-invasive test → Faecal pancreatic elastase

Exam pearl:
Secretin stimulation test = gold standard assessment of pancreatic function.

Medicine-01.question: ৩২) Which one of the following is the Initial test for hepatitis C virus infection?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is HCV antibody. The initial screening test for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is detection of anti-HCV antibodies.

Diagnostic approach:

  1. Anti-HCV antibody test → Initial screening ✓

  2. HCV RNA (PCR) → Confirms active infection and measures viral load ✓

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Liver biopsy → Not used for initial diagnosis; may assess fibrosis in selected cases.

  • HCV-RNA → Confirmatory test after a positive antibody result, not the initial screening test.

  • LFTs → May be abnormal but cannot diagnose HCV infection.

High-yield Hepatitis recall:

Initial test for HCV → Anti-HCV antibody
Confirm active infection → HCV RNA PCR

Exam pearl:
Anti-HCV antibody is the first-line screening test for hepatitis C infection.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৩) Hepatomegaly is common when the cirrhosis is due to which of the following codition?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Alcohol-related cirrhosis. Hepatomegaly is commonly seen in alcoholic cirrhosis due to ongoing inflammation, fatty change, and enlargement of hepatocytes.

Features:

  • Alcoholic cirrhosis → Often associated with hepatomegaly ✓

  • Later stages may develop a small, shrunken liver due to fibrosis.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Chronic viral hepatitis (B or C) → Cirrhotic liver is often small and shrunken, especially in established disease.

  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) → Can cause hepatomegaly in the fatty liver/NASH stage, but less classically associated with cirrhosis-related hepatomegaly.

  • Cystic fibrosis → May cause biliary cirrhosis, but hepatomegaly is not a classic association.

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Alcoholic liver disease → Hepatomegaly + fatty liver
Established cirrhosis → Small, nodular liver

Exam pearl:
Hepatomegaly in cirrhosis is classically associated with alcoholic cirrhosis.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৪) Which one of following is the most common cause of liver cirrhosis?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is chronic viral hepatitis (HBV or HCV). Globally, chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C infections are among the most common causes of liver cirrhosis.

Major causes of liver cirrhosis:

  • Chronic viral hepatitis (HBV/HCV) ✓ (commonest worldwide)

  • Alcohol-related liver disease

  • Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)

  • Autoimmune hepatitis

  • Cholestatic liver diseases (PBC, PSC)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Alcohol → A major cause in many Western countries, but not the most common global cause.

  • NAFLD → Increasing rapidly and may become a leading cause in some populations, but traditionally not the commonest worldwide.

  • Cystic fibrosis → Rare cause of biliary cirrhosis.

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Commonest cause of cirrhosis worldwide → Chronic HBV/HCV infection
Commonest cause in many Western countries → Alcohol-related liver disease

Exam pearl:
Chronic viral hepatitis remains the leading global cause of liver cirrhosis.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৫) Hepatitis E virus transmits through which of the following routes?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is faeces. Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is transmitted mainly by the faecal–oral route, usually through ingestion of contaminated water or food.

Key points:

  • Transmission: Faecal–oral route ✓

  • Common in areas with poor sanitation

  • Can cause outbreaks due to contaminated water

  • Severe disease may occur in pregnant women

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Blood → Common route for HBV, HCV, and HDV, not the main route for HEV.

  • Saliva → Not a recognised major route of HEV transmission.

  • Vertical → HEV can rarely transmit from mother to fetus, but it is not the primary route.

High-yield Hepatitis recall:

Virus Main transmission
HAV Faecal–oral
HEV Faecal–oral
HBV Blood, sexual, vertical
HCV Blood
HDV Blood (requires HBV)

Exam pearl:
Hepatitis E = Enteric transmission (faecal–oral route).

Medicine-01.question: ৩৬) Which of the following virus belongs to the picornavirus group of enteroviruses?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Hepatitis A virus (HAV). HAV belongs to the Picornaviridae family and is classified as an enterovirus.

Key points:

  • HAV

    • Family: Picornaviridae

    • Genus: Hepatovirus

    • Transmission: Faecal–oral route

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) → Family Hepadnaviridae (DNA virus)

  • Hepatitis C virus (HCV) → Family Flaviviridae

  • Hepatitis E virus (HEV) → Family Hepeviridae

High-yield Virology recall:

Picornavirus → HAV
Hepadnavirus → HBV
Flavivirus → HCV
Hepevirus → HEV

Exam pearl:
Hepatitis A is the only hepatitis virus classified as a picornavirus (enterovirus).

Medicine-01.question: ৩৭) Evidence of recent infection is best assessed by which of the following bio-marker?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Anti-HBc IgM. IgM antibody against hepatitis B core antigen is the best marker of recent or acute HBV infection.

HBV serological markers:

  • Anti-HBc IgM ✓ → Indicates recent acute infection (window period marker)

  • HBsAg → Indicates current HBV infection (acute or chronic)

  • HBeAg → Indicates active viral replication and high infectivity

  • Anti-HBe antibody → Indicates reduced viral replication/infectivity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • HBsAg → Appears early but cannot differentiate acute from chronic infection.

  • HBeAg → Reflects infectivity, not timing of infection.

  • Anti-HBe Ab → Suggests seroconversion and reduced replication.

High-yield Hepatitis B recall:

Recent HBV infection → Anti-HBc IgM
Chronic HBV infection → HBsAg >6 months
High infectivity → HBeAg positive

Exam pearl:
Anti-HBc IgM is the best evidence of recent acute hepatitis B infection.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৮) Hepatitis B virus mainly transmits through which of the following routes?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is vertical transmission. Globally, mother-to-child transmission (especially during the perinatal period) is the major route of HBV transmission in high-prevalence areas.

Major routes of HBV transmission:

  • Vertical transmission (mother → baby) ✓ (major route in endemic regions)

  • Sexual transmission

  • Blood exposure (injection drug use, contaminated blood products)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Injection drug use → Important route, especially in low-prevalence countries.

  • Sexual transmission → Common in adults but not the predominant global route.

  • Infected unscreened blood products → Can transmit HBV but is reduced due to blood screening.

High-yield Hepatitis B recall:

HBV transmission:

  • Endemic areas → Vertical/perinatal transmission

  • Developed countries → Sexual transmission and injection drug use

Exam pearl:
The main route of HBV spread worldwide is vertical transmission.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৯) After immunization of Hepatitis B virus infection which of the serological test become positive?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Anti-HBs. After hepatitis B vaccination, the body produces antibodies against the surface antigen, resulting in a positive Anti-HBs test.

Serological pattern after HBV immunization:

  • Anti-HBs positive ✓ → Indicates immunity due to vaccination

The other options are incorrect because:

  • HBsAg → Indicates current HBV infection, not vaccination.

  • Anti-HBc IgM → Indicates recent acute HBV infection.

  • Anti-HBc IgG → Indicates previous natural infection (not vaccination).

High-yield Hepatitis B recall:

Situation Positive marker
Vaccination Anti-HBs only
Acute infection HBsAg + Anti-HBc IgM
Past infection Anti-HBs + Anti-HBc IgG
Chronic infection HBsAg + Anti-HBc IgG

Exam pearl:
HBV vaccine → Anti-HBs positive, Anti-HBc negative.

Medicine-01.question: ৪০) Among Hepatotopic viruses which concern with major risk factor for developing HCC?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Hepatitis B virus (HBV). Chronic HBV infection is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Key points:

  • HBV can cause HCC even without cirrhosis due to direct oncogenic effects of viral DNA integration into hepatocytes.

  • Chronic HBV infection is one of the strongest risk factors for HCC worldwide.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hepatitis A → Causes acute hepatitis only; does not cause chronic infection or HCC.

  • Hepatitis C → Strong risk factor for HCC, mainly through chronic inflammation and cirrhosis, but HBV is the classic major viral risk factor.

  • Hepatitis E → Causes acute hepatitis; chronic infection is uncommon (except in immunosuppressed patients).

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Major viral risk factor for HCC → Chronic Hepatitis B
HCV → HCC mainly through cirrhosis

Exam pearl:
HBV is the hepatitis virus most strongly associated with hepatocellular carcinoma.

Medicine-01.question: ৪১) The most common organism responsible for Pyogenic liver abscess?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Escherichia coli (E. coli). E. coli is the most common organism causing pyogenic liver abscess, especially in cases arising from biliary tract infection or portal spread.

Common organisms in pyogenic liver abscess:

  • E. coli ✓ (most common)

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae (important cause, especially in diabetic patients)

  • Streptococcus species

  • Staphylococcus aureus

  • Anaerobes (e.g., Bacteroides)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. aureus → Can cause liver abscess, especially with bacteraemia, but less common.

  • Bacteroides → Anaerobic organism associated with abscess formation but not the most common.

  • S. epidermidis → Mainly associated with prosthetic device infections.

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Pyogenic liver abscess → E. coli (most common)
Diabetes + liver abscess → Think Klebsiella

Exam pearl:
E. coli is the leading organism responsible for pyogenic liver abscess.

Medicine-01.question: ৪২) Abdominal pain is the most common symptom of liver abscess which usually in which of the following areas of the liver?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is right upper quadrant (RUQ). Liver abscess most commonly involves the right lobe of the liver, producing pain in the right upper quadrant.

Key points:

  • Right lobe of liver → most common site of abscess ✓

  • Pain may radiate to:

    • Right shoulder (diaphragmatic irritation)

    • Right scapular region

  • Associated features:

    • Fever

    • Tender hepatomegaly

    • Right upper quadrant pain

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Right lower quadrant → Suggests appendicular or ileocaecal pathology.

  • Left upper quadrant → Less common as left lobe involvement is less frequent.

  • Left lower quadrant → Not typical for liver pathology.

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Liver abscess → Right lobe + RUQ pain
Amoebic liver abscess → Right lobe most commonly affected

Exam pearl:
Most liver abscesses occur in the right lobe and present with right upper quadrant pain.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৩) Which of the following is the most revealing investigation for diagnosis of liver abscess?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is ultrasonography (USG). USG is the most useful and commonly used investigation for detecting liver abscess because it can directly demonstrate the abscess cavity and guide aspiration.

Role of investigations:

  • USG ✓

    • Detects liver abscess

    • Determines size and location

    • Helps guide drainage/aspiration

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CBC → May show leukocytosis but is not diagnostic.

  • LFT → May be abnormal but cannot confirm liver abscess.

  • Liver biopsy → Not routinely used; invasive and unnecessary for diagnosis.

High-yield Hepatology recall:

Best initial/most revealing test for liver abscess → USG
CT scan → More sensitive, especially for small or complicated abscesses

Exam pearl:
Ultrasound is the investigation of choice for diagnosis of liver abscess.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৪) Early lethality, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, small head, frequent congenital heart disease. These features are associated with which of the following genetic disorder?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Patau’s syndrome (Trisomy 13). Patau syndrome is characterized by severe congenital abnormalities, early lethality, cleft lip and palate, polydactyly, microcephaly, and congenital heart defects.

Features of Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13):

  • Cleft lip and palate ✓

  • Postaxial polydactyly ✓

  • Microcephaly ✓

  • Congenital heart disease ✓

  • Severe developmental impairment

  • High infant mortality

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21) → Characteristic features include intellectual disability, flat facial profile, single palmar crease, and congenital heart disease (especially AV septal defect), but not typically cleft lip/palate or polydactyly.

  • Edwards’ syndrome (Trisomy 18) → Features include clenched fists with overlapping fingers, rocker-bottom feet, micrognathia, and severe growth restriction.

  • Klinefelter’s syndrome (47,XXY) → Male hypogonadism, tall stature, infertility, and small testes.

High-yield Genetics recall:

Syndrome Key clue
Patau (Trisomy 13) Cleft lip/palate + Polydactyly
Edwards (Trisomy 18) Clenched fists + rocker-bottom feet
Down (Trisomy 21) AVSD + intellectual disability

Exam pearl:
Trisomy 13 = “Patau → Polydactyly + Palate defect.”

Medicine-01.question: ৪৫) Which one of the followings is the Numerical chromosomal abnormalities?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Turner’s syndrome (45,X). Turner syndrome is a numerical chromosomal abnormality caused by monosomy of the X chromosome.

Key points:

  • Turner syndrome:

    • Karyotype: 45,X

    • Loss of one X chromosome (monosomy)

    • Features:

      • Short stature

      • Webbed neck

      • Gonadal dysgenesis

      • Infertility

      • Coarctation of aorta

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Prader–Willi syndrome → Chromosomal imprinting disorder (loss of paternal chromosome 15 region), not numerical abnormality.

  • Angelman’s syndrome → Imprinting disorder (loss of maternal chromosome 15 region), not numerical abnormality.

  • DiGeorge syndrome → 22q11 deletion syndrome (structural chromosomal abnormality).

High-yield Genetics recall:

Numerical chromosomal abnormalities:

  • Down syndrome → Trisomy 21

  • Edwards syndrome → Trisomy 18

  • Patau syndrome → Trisomy 13

  • Turner syndrome → 45,X

  • Klinefelter syndrome → 47,XXY

Exam pearl:
Turner syndrome is a classic numerical chromosomal abnormality (monosomy X).

Medicine-01.question: ৪৬) Autosomal dominant condition
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is Neurofibromatosis. Neurofibromatosis (especially NF1) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutation in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17.

Features of Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1):

  • Café-au-lait spots

  • Neurofibromas

  • Lisch nodules

  • Axillary freckling

  • Increased risk of optic pathway glioma

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Haemochromatosis → Usually autosomal recessive (HFE gene mutation).

  • Wilson’s disease → Autosomal recessive (ATP7B mutation).

  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency → Autosomal recessive (SERPINA1 mutation).

High-yield Genetics recall:

Autosomal dominant:

  • Neurofibromatosis

  • Marfan syndrome

  • Huntington disease

  • Familial hypercholesterolaemia

  • Adult polycystic kidney disease

Autosomal recessive:

  • Haemochromatosis

  • Wilson disease

  • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

  • Cystic fibrosis

Medicine-01.question: ৪৭) Haemophilia
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is X-linked recessive condition. Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and haemophilia B (factor IX deficiency) are inherited as X-linked recessive disorders.

Key points:

  • Gene defect is located on the X chromosome

  • Mainly affects males (XY) because they have only one X chromosome

  • Females are usually carriers (XX)

Inheritance pattern:

  • Carrier mother → affected son

  • Affected father → passes the defective X chromosome to all daughters (carriers), not sons

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Autosomal dominant → Seen in conditions like Marfan syndrome and Huntington disease.

  • Autosomal recessive → Seen in cystic fibrosis, Wilson disease, haemochromatosis.

  • X-linked dominant → Seen in conditions like vitamin D–resistant rickets.

High-yield Genetics recall:

X-linked recessive:

  • Haemophilia A & B

  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy

  • G6PD deficiency

  • Red-green colour blindness

Exam pearl:
Haemophilia = X-linked recessive inheritance.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৮) Gene therapy is the treatment option for which of the following condition?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is all above. Gene therapy has potential applications in inherited disorders, cancer, and cardiovascular diseases.

Examples:

  • Cystic fibrosis ✓

    • Gene therapy aims to replace the defective CFTR gene.

  • Cancer ✓

    • Used in approaches such as:

      • Tumour suppressor gene replacement

      • CAR-T cell therapy

      • Oncolytic viral therapy

  • Cardiovascular disease ✓

    • Investigated for:

      • Therapeutic angiogenesis

      • Gene transfer to promote new blood vessel formation

The other options are not exclusive because gene therapy is a broad therapeutic strategy used in multiple disease categories.

High-yield Genetics recall:

Gene therapy applications:

  • Inherited disorders → Cystic fibrosis, SCID, haemophilia

  • Cancer → CAR-T, gene-modified immune cells

  • Cardiovascular disease → Angiogenesis therapy

Exam pearl:
Gene therapy is applicable to genetic disorders, malignancy, and cardiovascular diseases.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৯) Which durug causes dyspepsia?
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is NSAIDs. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) commonly cause dyspepsia by irritating the gastric mucosa and inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis.

Mechanism:

  • NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes

  • ↓ Prostaglandin production

  • ↓ Gastric mucus and bicarbonate secretion

  • ↓ Mucosal protection

  • Leads to dyspepsia, gastritis, peptic ulceration

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Domperidone → Prokinetic drug used to treat nausea, vomiting, and dyspeptic symptoms.

  • PPI → Reduces acid secretion and is used in treatment of dyspepsia and acid-related disorders.

  • Sodium alginate → Forms a protective barrier and is used for reflux symptoms.

High-yield GI recall:

Drug causing dyspepsia → NSAIDs
NSAIDs → Gastritis + Peptic ulcer + GI bleeding

Exam pearl:
NSAIDs are common causes of drug-induced dyspepsia.

Medicine-01.question: ৫০) Amount of fluid excreated from the body through stool is..
Medicine-01.exp:
The correct answer is 150 ml. Normal daily stool contains approximately 100–200 ml of water, with an average value of about 150 ml.

Normal fluid balance in the gastrointestinal tract:

  • Fluid entering GIT daily ≈ 8–10 L

  • Most is absorbed in the small intestine and colon

  • Water lost in stool ≈ 100–200 ml/day

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 100 ml → Within normal range but lower than the average value.

  • 350 ml → Higher than normal.

  • 500 ml → Suggests increased stool water loss, as seen in diarrhoea.

High-yield GI recall:

Normal stool water loss → ~150 ml/day
Diarrhoea → increased stool water loss

Exam pearl:
Normal faecal water excretion is approximately 150 ml per day.
